prompt.context: Our client is a winery located in California and they sell wine all over the US. They produce various marketing materials to be used in the displays in stores where their wines are sold. These marketing materials are either pushed by the central Corporate Marketing team or pulled by regional sales field offices. These marketing materials are stored in a central warehouse in Chicago and over time a lot of obsolete materials have been accumulated.
prompt.question: Our client needs your help in reducing obsolete materials and improving their bottom line. How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.q: How much does the client currently spend on marketing materials?
clarifying_info.a: The client spends $20 million on marketing materials — $3 million in freight and $17 million in materials.
The corporate marketing team pushes materials out without asking field sales teams. Regional field sales teams can pull materials when needed.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current inventory level?
clarifying_info.a: The current inventory in Chicago is $17 million and is not expected to grow in the future.

clarifying_info.q: What are the current inventory holding costs?
clarifying_info.a: Inventory holding costs are $1 million per year for $8.5 million of inventory.

exhibits.title: Suppliers of Wine Marketing Materials
exhibits.shows: A map of the US showing the geographic distribution of suppliers of wine marketing materials, segmented by region with Chicago marked as the warehouse location

exhibits.title: Retailers of Wine using the Marketing Materials
exhibits.shows: A map of the US showing the geographic distribution of wine retailers that receive the marketing materials, segmented by region with Chicago marked as the warehouse location

framework: External analysis — Competitors: Are competitors using marketing materials similarly? Customers: Are customers responsive to the materials? Suppliers: Are marketing material suppliers efficient and on-time?

Internal analysis — Corporate Marketing Team: How are materials pushed out? Is forecasting accurate? Field Sales Teams: How are materials pulled? Is field forecasting more accurate given local market knowledge?
Supply chain / network optimization — Evaluate warehouse location relative to supplier and retailer concentrations; consider adding or relocating warehouses
Cost-benefit analysis of third-party inventory management platform

questions.prompt: What are the root causes of obsolete marketing materials accumulating in the Chicago warehouse?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify the push vs. pull imbalance: the corporate marketing team forecasts and pushes materials without input from field sales, leading to inaccurate demand forecasting and excess inventory. Field sales teams are closer to local markets and better positioned to forecast what materials are actually needed. External factors (competitors, suppliers) are secondary; the core issue is internal misalignment between corporate and field.

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit I (supplier map) and Exhibit II (retailer map), what do you observe, and what supply chain optimizations would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Key observations: (1) Suppliers are concentrated in the Southwest (37%) and West (28%), far from the Chicago warehouse. (2) Retailers are also concentrated in the Southwest (27%) and West (28%), with significant Midwest presence (20%). The warehouse in Chicago is geographically misaligned with both the bulk of suppliers and the bulk of retailers. Recommendations: (a) Add a second warehouse between the West and Southwest regions to reduce freight costs and lead times; (b) Move the warehouse to the Southwest to be more central to supplier and retailer concentrations; (c) Consolidate or shift suppliers to be closer to the warehouse. Each option requires a cost-benefit analysis.

questions.prompt: A third-party operator has offered to install a web-based platform to manage inventory for $5 million. The platform will reduce Chicago warehouse inventory by 50% and reduce inventory holding costs by 10%. Should the client accept this deal?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure a benefits vs. costs analysis, quantify year-1 net benefit, and note the benefit continues in future years. Strong candidates also mention considering alternatives (other vendors or in-house solution) that might deliver greater benefits at lower cost.

math.setup: Current inventory = $17MM. Inventory reduction = 50% (one-time). Holding costs = $1MM/year for $8.5MM inventory; reduced by 10%. Cost of platform = $5MM.
steps: Holding cost savings of $0.1MM/year continue in perpetuity
math.answer: Yes, accept the deal. Year-1 benefits ($8.6MM) outweigh the cost ($5MM) by $3.6MM, and $0.1MM/year in holding cost savings continue going forward. However, the client should also evaluate alternative providers and an in-house solution, which may deliver even greater benefits.

brainstorming.prompt: What ideas do you have for increasing profitability in this situation?

categories.name: External — Competitors
ideas: Benchmark whether competitors use similar marketing material push/pull models
Assess whether competitor marketing material strategies drive better sell-through

categories.name: External — Customers
ideas: Determine whether retailers and end consumers actually respond to these materials
Assess whether the wrong mix of materials is being produced for each market

categories.name: External — Suppliers
ideas: Evaluate whether current suppliers are delivering on time
Assess whether supplier fragmentation is driving higher costs

categories.name: Internal — Corporate Marketing Team
ideas: Audit accuracy of corporate forecasting for material demand
Evaluate whether push model should be replaced or reduced in favor of field-pull
Reduce production of materials that consistently become obsolete

categories.name: Internal — Field Sales Teams
ideas: Empower regional teams to pull materials based on local demand signals
Increase field sales input into marketing material planning cycles
Share field forecasting data with corporate to improve overall accuracy

categories.name: Supply Chain / Network
ideas: Relocate warehouse to Southwest to align with supplier and retailer concentrations
Add a second warehouse in the West/Southwest corridor
Consolidate suppliers geographically closer to warehouse(s)
Implement inventory management platform to reduce stock and holding costs

recommendation: Rebalance the corporate push vs. field-pull model for marketing materials — give regional field sales teams more authority and input to reduce over-production and obsolescence
Conduct a cost-benefit analysis on warehouse relocation or adding a second warehouse in the West/Southwest given the geographic concentration of both suppliers and retailers
Accept the third-party web-based inventory platform offer ($5MM cost vs. $8.6MM Year-1 benefit), but first evaluate alternative providers and an in-house build to ensure best value
risks: Changing warehouse location or adding a second warehouse involves significant upfront capital costs and operational disruption
Dependence on a third-party operator for supply chain management introduces vendor risk and reduces control
Forecasting improvements take time; there may be a lag before obsolete inventory levels decline materially
next_steps: Conduct detailed cost-benefit analysis for warehouse relocation vs. adding a second distribution center
Issue RFP to multiple inventory management platform vendors before committing to the $5MM offer
Pilot a field-sales-led pull model in one region to measure impact on obsolescence rates before rolling out nationally
